title: Your Teen's Friends May Shape Their Mental Health More Than You Think — A 600,000-Person Study Shows How
excerpt: A massive Finnish study published in JAMA Psychiatry finds that adolescents whose peers have mental health diagnoses are significantly more likely to develop conditions like anxiety and depression themselves — a finding with urgent implications for diaspora families navigating unfamiliar school systems.
body:
If you are raising a teenager in the United States, Canada or the United Kingdom, here is a number worth sitting with: more than 600,000.

That is how many young people were tracked in a sweeping new study from Finland, published this week in *JAMA Psychiatry*, one of the world's most respected psychiatric journals. The researchers followed an entire generation — millennials and early Gen Z born between 1985 and 2000 — using nationwide health records and school enrolment data to answer a deceptively simple question: does your teenager's mental health depend, in part, on the mental health of the kids around them?

The answer, it turns out, is a clear yes.

## What the Study Found

Adolescents whose school-year peers had been diagnosed with a mental health condition — anxiety, depression, substance use disorders — were significantly more likely to receive the same diagnosis themselves. The effect was strongest among teenagers attending the same school, rather than merely living in the same neighbourhood. And it intensified in later adolescence, precisely when peer relationships overtake parental influence as the dominant social force.

More strikingly, the risk wasn't limited to direct exposure. If a teen's peer had a *family member* with a mental health diagnosis — a parent or sibling with depression, say — the teen was also more likely to develop a similar condition. The researchers call this "social transmission," a term borrowed from epidemiology but applied here to the way emotions, behaviours and social norms ripple through peer networks over time.

## Not Contagious — but Influential

The researchers are careful to distinguish their findings from the idea that mental illness is "contagious." You cannot catch depression the way you catch a cold. Instead, the mechanism likely involves a mix of emotional contagion — the well-documented tendency to mirror the moods of those around us — and normalisation. When a peer opens up about struggling, it may lower the threshold for others to seek help, leading to more diagnoses in the group.

"For teenagers, peers are their most important and primary source of a sense of community and friendship — more than adults, and even more than their parents," Dr. Consuelo Cagande, division director for child and adolescent psychiatry at Northwell Health, told the New York Post. She theorises that being around someone who is depressed, even online, can trigger a genetic vulnerability in another teenager.

The study also found that the association was strongest in high school — a period that, in Finland as in most Western countries, coincides with heightened academic pressure, shifting peer relationships and intensifying identity formation.

## Why This Matters for Diaspora Families

For Indian parents in the West, these findings land with particular force. The diaspora family often operates at the intersection of two cultural scripts: one that prizes academic achievement, emotional restraint and family reputation, and another — the Western school environment — where mental health awareness is increasingly normalised and peer influence is pervasive.

The result can be a painful disconnect. A teenager whose school friends are openly discussing therapy may begin to examine their own emotional landscape in ways their parents never did at the same age. An NRI parent accustomed to treating anxiety as a phase or depression as a character flaw may miss the signals entirely.

The Finnish study suggests that the school environment itself — not just genetics, not just parenting — shapes mental health risk. For families who have moved countries, this is both a warning and an invitation: your child's peer ecosystem matters as much as what happens at home.

A 2023 report from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that anxiety diagnoses among American adolescents had increased from 13 per cent to 28 per cent over the previous 15 years, while suicide attempts among young people had doubled. South Asian-American teenagers, often navigating bicultural identity stress on top of standard adolescent pressures, are not immune.

## What Parents Can Do

The study's lead author, Jussi Alho of the University of Helsinki, emphasised that the findings point beyond individual risk to the wider environments young people inhabit. School-based mental health programs that harness the positive power of peer influence — rather than treating it as a threat — are key.

In Australia, a program called Mind Your Mate has already shown promise in lowering depression risk among teenagers through peer mental health education. Similar models are emerging in the US and UK.

For diaspora parents, the practical takeaway is straightforward but uncomfortable: know who your teenager's closest friends are, understand the mental health climate in their school, and resist the cultural impulse to dismiss emotional distress as weakness. The evidence now shows that the people around your child are shaping their mental health in measurable, significant ways — and pretending otherwise is no longer an option.

**Sources:** Alho et al., *JAMA Psychiatry* (2026); New York Post; Phys.org / The Conversation; SAMHSA National Survey on Drug Use and Health
